opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and I think it's one where the answer is probably going to be less clean than people would like.

A robot that's going to do useful things over long periods, like cleaning up a house or working in a kitchen for an hour, needs context at several different timescales. There's the very immediate stuff: where's my hand, what's the object I'm grasping, how is it moving. Then there's the medium-term stuff: I already wiped down this counter, the dishwasher is half loaded. And then there's the long-term stuff: this person likes the mugs on the left shelf, this drawer sticks.

I don't think the right answer is to hand-design a representation for each of those. That's been tried in robotics for a long time, with explicit maps, symbolic state, scene graphs, and it tends to be brittle because you have to anticipate in advance what matters. What's worked better in the last few years is letting the model figure out what to keep, the same way language models implicitly decide what in their context is relevant.

I do think language is going to play a big role, though, at least at the higher levels. Language is a remarkably compact way to represent the semantically meaningful parts of a task. If the robot can tell itself "I've finished the plates, now I'm doing the cups," that's an extremely efficient summary, much more efficient than keeping every image frame from the last ten minutes. We've seen in our own work with vision-language-action models that having the model produce intermediate textual reasoning or subtask predictions helps a lot with longer-horizon behavior.

But language alone isn't enough at the low level. How hard to press, how a cloth is draped, exactly where a cup's handle is: those things are very hard to verbalize, and they need to be represented in something more continuous and learned. So I imagine something hierarchical. There's a short, high-bandwidth visual and proprioceptive memory for fine control, and a longer, more compressed, probably partly linguistic memory for what's going on in the task and in the world.

The deeper point is that the representation should come out of learning, guided by what actually helps the robot succeed, rather than out of our intuitions about what the state of the world "is." In robotics, our intuitions about what matters have often been wrong, and the data tends to be a better teacher.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes compact linguistic summaries for task-level context from visual and proprioceptive memory for fine control.

r002.rationale: It says the model should decide what to keep based on relevance and what helps the robot succeed, implying the representation retains goal-relevant information.

r003.rationale: It includes proprioception alongside visual and linguistic information, showing that multimodal context extends beyond images and text.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions in robotics right now, and the answer has changed a lot even in the last few years.

The classical way of thinking about it was that you'd hand-design the representation. You'd say, okay, the robot needs to know where the objects are, so we'll have a pose estimator, and it needs to know the geometry of the scene, so we'll build a map, and then planning happens on top of those explicit symbols. And that works in narrow settings, but it fails in exactly the way you'd expect, which is that the world has way more stuff in it than you anticipated when you designed the representation. The robot encounters a situation where the relevant context is something you didn't think to encode, and it just has no way to handle it.

So the view I've come around to, and I think the evidence is increasingly pointing this way, is that the representation should be learned, and it should be learned from as broad a source of experience as possible. The reason is that what counts as relevant context is itself task dependent and situation dependent. If I'm picking up a cup, the relevant context might be whether it's full, whether it's hot, whether someone is about to reach for it. You can't enumerate that. But a model that has been trained on a lot of data about how the world works will have, embedded in its representation, some notion of which features matter in which situations.

Now, where it gets interesting is the role of language and vision-language models. One thing we've found in the work on things like RT-2 and more recently with the vision-language-action models is that if you build on top of a model that was pretrained on internet-scale data, you get a lot of semantic context for free. The robot knows what a "trash can" is or what "fragile" means, not because anyone told it in a robotics dataset, but because that knowledge is sitting in the backbone. So in some sense the representation of context is being inherited from a model that already learned a lot about the human world.

But I'd caution against thinking language is the whole answer. Language is a great interface and a great source of prior knowledge, but a lot of what a robot needs to know about its situation is not linguistic. It's the physical stuff. How much friction is there, is this thing going to tip, how far have I inserted this peg. That's the part that has to come from robotic experience, from actually interacting with the world. So I think the right picture is something like a representation that's grounded in the semantic priors you get from large pretrained models, but then refined and extended through embodied data, through the robot's own interactions.

And the last piece I'd add is memory and history. A lot of the context the robot needs isn't visible in the current observation at all. It's what happened five seconds ago or five minutes ago. Did I already check this drawer? Did the person say they wanted the red one? So increasingly the representation needs to be something that can integrate over time, and I think the honest answer is that we're still figuring out how to do that well in robotics, especially when the data is as scarce as it is relative to language.

r001.rationale: It contrasts explicit symbols and maps or geometry with language-based semantic knowledge and physical context grounded in robot interaction.

r002.rationale: It says relevant context depends on the task and situation, but does not clearly state that the representation should preserve only information needed to achieve the goal.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes language priors from physical knowledge gained through interaction, but does not state that multimodality extends beyond combining images and text.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that the context shouldn't just be a description of what the robot sees right now. It needs to capture the things that matter for deciding what to do, and some of those things might have happened quite a while ago.

Suppose you ask a robot to make you a cup of coffee. It opens a cabinet, sees that there aren't any mugs there, and closes it. That observation needs to persist somehow. If its context is just the current camera image, it's going to keep opening the same cabinet. But it probably doesn't need to remember every pixel of what was inside. It needs to remember something like, “I checked this cabinet; the mugs aren't there.”

Language is a useful representation for that kind of information. It's compact, and it lets you connect observations to a task. But I don't think language alone is sufficient. If you're trying to grasp a cup, the precise geometry of the handle matters, and describing that geometry in words would be a very awkward way to control your hand.

So I would expect a combination: some representations that preserve spatial and physical detail, and others that summarize events, instructions, and what you've learned about the world. The interesting question is how much of that structure we should design, and how much can emerge from training a system to accomplish tasks. I'd lean toward learning a lot of it, because what makes a memory useful is ultimately whether it helps you choose the right action later.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language as a compact way to summarize events and instructions with representations that preserve spatial and physical detail for tasks like grasping.

r002.rationale: It says context should capture what matters for deciding what to do and need not preserve every pixel, illustrated by remembering only that a cabinet was checked and had no mugs.

r003.rationale: The response proposes combining language with spatial and physical detail, but does not state that multimodality extends beyond combining images and text.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to think about context is in terms of what the robot needs to predict in order to act. If I’m trying to pick up a cup, I need to know where the cup is, but I might also need to know whether it’s full, whether it’s fragile, or whether somebody is about to move it. Those things aren’t necessarily captured by a geometric map of the world.

So I would lean toward learning representations through the task of predicting the consequences of actions. The representation should preserve the distinctions that matter for choosing what to do. And some of those distinctions require history. If you saw somebody put an object in a drawer, you should remember that even though the object is no longer visible.

Language can be a useful part of this. It gives you a compact way to express goals and certain kinds of knowledge. But it’s hard to imagine that everything a robot needs to know should pass through a language description. Think about the information you use when you’re catching something or adjusting your grip. You don’t describe all of that to yourself in words.

The interesting question is how to learn a system that brings together those different timescales: the immediate sensory information, the things it remembers from a few minutes ago, and the more general knowledge it has acquired across many tasks. I don’t think we know the right architecture for that yet. But grounding that representation in action—what information actually helps you accomplish the goal—seems like a very good starting point.

r001.rationale: It contrasts language as a way to express goals and knowledge with geometric maps and sensory information.

r002.rationale: It says the representation should preserve distinctions that matter for choosing actions and information that helps accomplish the goal.

r003.rationale: It mentions language, sensory input, memory, and learned knowledge, but does not clearly state that multimodality extends beyond combining images and text.
